subject: community-medicine
title: Health Communication: Process, Barriers, and Education Approaches

steps.title: Elements of the communication process
steps.tx: Every health message travels the **communication process**: a communicator encodes an idea into a message, sends it through a channel to an audience, whose decoding and feedback complete or break the loop. Feedback distinguishes communication from mere transmission; without it the health worker broadcasts blind. The audience's response (questions, adoption, rumours returning) is programme data, not noise.
steps.say: Communicator, message, channel, audience, feedback: the loop closes only when feedback returns. Without feedback you are broadcasting blind.

nodes.label: Channel carries it to the audience

steps.title: Barriers to communication
steps.tx: **Barriers to health communication** stack at every element: physiological (deafness, illness), psychological (fear, prejudice, selective listening), environmental (noise, distance), semantic (jargon, language mismatch), and cultural (taboos around contraception or mental illness). Naming the barrier chooses the remedy: interpreters for language, privacy for taboo, repetition and demonstration for low literacy, quiet rooms for counselling.
steps.say: Barriers hide in the sender, message, channel, and receiver. Diagnose which one before prescribing louder repetition.

steps.title: Approaches to health education
steps.tx: Three classical **approaches to health education** differ in power flow: the regulatory approach compels by law (seat belts, smoke free rules), the service approach supplies facilities and waits (clinics alone, historically disappointing), and the educational approach informs and motivates voluntary change, slowest but most durable. Modern programmes blend all three, reserving compulsion for risks imposed on others.
steps.say: Law compels, services wait, education persuades. Durable change blends them, with education carrying the long term load.

steps.title: Principles of health education
steps.tx: Field tested **principles of health education** include credibility of the messenger, interest anchored in felt needs, participation of the audience, motivation, comprehension in local language, reinforcement by repetition, learning by doing, proceeding from known to unknown and concrete to abstract, setting an example, good human relations, and feedback. Violating participation (lecturing at silent villagers) is the commonest programme failure mode.
steps.say: Start from felt needs, use local language, make people participate and practise. Lectures without participation rarely change behaviour.

nodes.label: Anchor in felt need and known facts

steps.title: Audio visual aids: choosing by purpose
steps.tx: **Audio visual aids in health education** divide into auditory (radio, announcements), visual projected (slides, films), visual non projected (posters, flip charts, flashcards, models), and combined (television, video, demonstrations). The cone of experience teaches that doing outlasts seeing, which outlasts hearing: a mother who practises preparing oral rehydration solution remembers it when the diarrhoea comes at midnight.
steps.say: Doing beats seeing beats hearing. Let mothers mix the solution themselves instead of only watching your demonstration.

rows: Single message reminder at point of action
Skills: ORS mixing, hand washing, breastfeeding

steps.tx: An ASHA mixes **oral rehydration solution** in front of a mothers' group, then asks one mother to repeat the steps herself. That return demonstration is the combined method that outlasts a poster or a radio message, because doing is retained longer than seeing or hearing. Measuring the packet into the stated volume of clean water, stirring, and tasting fixes the sequence. When diarrhoea begins at midnight, the mother who practised can prepare the drink without waiting for a clinic.

steps.title: Focus group discussion
steps.tx: A **focus group discussion** gathers six to twelve homogeneous participants with a trained moderator and a guide of open questions to surface beliefs, rumours, and language around a topic (why mothers fear injections, why men avoid vasectomy). It researches and persuades simultaneously but generalises cautiously; findings guide message design and pretesting rather than estimating population percentages.
steps.say: Six to twelve similar people, one skilled moderator, open questions. Focus groups reveal why, never how many.

steps.title: Role play and demonstration methods
steps.tx: **Role play in health education** lets participants enact real encounters (refusing a drink, negotiating condom use, counselling a defaulter mother) then debrief feelings and alternatives safely. Demonstration with return demonstration builds psychomotor skill. Both convert passive audiences into rehearsed actors, which is why training of community workers relies on them far more than on lectures.
steps.say: Role play rehearses real life safely. People who have practised refusal or counselling actually do it later.

steps.title: Counselling versus health education
steps.tx: Though cousins, **counselling and health education differ**: education addresses groups toward general behaviour, while counselling is a private, client centred dialogue helping one person decide (contraceptive choice, HIV test consent, infant feeding with HIV). Counselling demands listening, confidentiality, and non directive support; its Indian programme face is the counsellor cadre in ICTC (integrated counselling and testing centres) and family planning services.
steps.say: Education speaks to groups; counselling sits with one person's decision. Listening and confidentiality define the second.

rows: Group or public versus one client or couple
Clear messaging versus listening and empathy

steps.title: IEC and BCC in programmes
steps.tx: Programme vocabulary separates **information education communication (IEC)** materials and campaigns from behaviour change communication (BCC), which researches barriers and facilitators, segments audiences, and engineers environments (not just messages) toward specific behaviours. The newer umbrella, social and behaviour change communication, adds social norms and community mobilisation. Examiners test IEC as the older material centred term against BCC as the behaviour centred successor.
steps.say: IEC makes materials; BCC engineers behaviour change. Modern programmes fund the second and measure behaviour, not posters.
